l: AudioPhysx — audio that reacts to the world
p: A MetaSound and Blueprint toolkit for responsive, carefully designed Unreal Engine audio. AudioPhysx brings together flexible sample players, physically inspired processing, propagation tools and control utilities so you can make sounds respond to distance, material, movement and gameplay events without duplicating the same large node graph everywhere.

The plugin is designed around an important distinction: the game provides what happened and where, while the audio graph decides which recording is appropriate and how it should sound. Sometimes the best solution is a believable physical approximation; sometimes it is a deliberate, well-authored variation of a recording. The two approaches can work together.

The pages describe the newly uploaded UE 5.8.4 stereo source, including the RPM-enabled Start Loop End Player and the new Stereo to Mono converter. These are source-verified interfaces, not proof that every node has been compiled and tested in a packaged Shipping build. See compatibility before making release claims.

Playback tools handle the details that become repetitive in ordinary graphs: non-identical one-shots, shuffle-bag history, fixed and random sequences, synchronized layers, physical-material routing and held actions with proper endings. For example, the Start Loop End Player can schedule overlapping gunshot variations from a real RPM value while preserving a release tail when the player stops firing.

Acoustic tools take meaningful data from the world and transform the sound rather than guessing geometry from audio samples. Material Transmission filters sound that passes through barriers; Acoustic Paths renders one world-selected route; Early Reflections adds a lightweight sense of local space; Source Directivity can make the front of a speaker sound different from its rear. Each tool has its own purpose and limitations, explained in its reference page.

Stereo is now a first-class signal path. The playback and stereo DSP nodes provide Out Left and Out Right, preserving genuine channel differences. If the final sound should become a mono point-source emitter, AP: Stereo to Mono performs an explicit fold-down. The format decision belongs to the sound designer rather than being forced by every intermediate node. Read the stereo guide.

l: How to get a convincing result
p: Start with good source recordings and one clear goal. Choose a player that solves the required event timing, then add only processing that supplies a distinct audible benefit. A distance-based selection, a Doppler effect and a wall-transmission filter are three different tools; none automatically fixes an inaccurate listener position or a poorly edited Wave Asset. AudioPhysx aims to make these decisions approachable without pretending that every source must use every processor.

For a first exercise, follow your first MetaSound. If you already know MetaSounds, go straight to the node library. You can also browse examples or check troubleshooting when an installed graph does not behave as expected.

The fastest way to understand AudioPhysx is to make one sound work end to end before building a complicated acoustic system. You can begin with an ordinary imported recording, one trigger and a stereo MetaSound Source. Once the basic signal flows correctly, it becomes much easier to understand why a material-aware player, propagation processor or world-query component is useful.

This documentation uses the current stereo C++ source as its contract. An older MetaSound graph may still have Out Mono pins from a previous version of the plugin; those assets should be backed up and migrated deliberately rather than resaved as soon as Unreal refreshes their nodes.

Begin with installation. Confirm that the AudioPhysx plugin loads and the node categories appear in the MetaSound editor. Then read requirements and terminology for the difference between Wave Assets, audio buffers, control values and triggers. These distinctions prevent many silent-graph problems later.

Build your first MetaSound. The tutorial uses Sequence Wave Player because it demonstrates how playback timing and completion work without needing gameplay path queries or project-wide acoustic settings. After that, the stereo routing guide explains how to keep Left and Right channels or fold them down to mono for appropriate 3D sources.

Add game integration when the sound needs it. The Blueprint section explains how to obtain the physical material from a hit, submit a projectile path, and query a selected acoustic route. These calculations are useful, but they should not be made prerequisites for a simple random or layered sound effect.
If something does not play, use the setup checklist and troubleshooting. It is usually faster to isolate one missing Wave Asset or trigger than to adjust ten unrelated DSP settings.

AudioPhysx is a native C++ plugin for Unreal Engine. The code reviewed for this edition targets UE 5.8.4 and includes the stereo conversion and RPM playback system. That establishes what the source is intended to build against; it does not prove that a final Fab distribution has passed testing in every target build configuration. For current support claims, consult the compatibility page.

You need a compatible Unreal project with MetaSounds enabled, the complete AudioPhysx plugin installed and some legal Wave Assets for the tutorials. More advanced systems require meaningful game data: a projectile path, an impact location, source-listener separation, a hit Physical Material or an acoustic barrier and portal setup. The audio nodes cannot invent those values from a waveform alone.

A Wave Asset is a reference to an imported recording. A Wave Asset Array stores several recordings for variation, selection or layering. The array itself is not an audio stream; a Wave Player decides what to do with its contents when an event arrives.

An audio buffer carries actual samples. With the current stereo AudioPhysx convention, you normally connect the Left audio channel to the Left input of the next processor, and Right to Right. The final MetaSound Source output format should match the signal you want to render. If you intentionally need one mono stream, Stereo to Mono makes that conversion explicit.

A Trigger represents a point in time: play, stop, release, reset or announce completion. Triggers are not audio signals. A Float, Boolean, Integer, String or Float Array is a control value; it can describe distance, acoustic loss, random probability or surface identity without being either an event or an audio channel.

Most Unreal world coordinates and many AudioPhysx distances are expressed in centimetres. Other pins are explicitly labelled metres (m), metres per second (m/s), milliseconds (ms), seconds (s), decibels (dB), hertz (Hz), kilopascals (kPa) or semitones (st). Use the unit printed on the pin, because there is no universal convention that all values in the plugin are metres.

For example, a projectile whose closest approach is 500 Unreal units away is usually 500 cm, or 5 m. Feeding the number 500 to the flyby player's Distance (m) would tell it the projectile passed half a kilometre away. Likewise, a pitch ratio from Doppler Ratio is not interchangeable with a semitone pitch input.
If an effect sounds unexpectedly late, quiet or bright, verify the values and units before changing the DSP. Errors in source data can be far more dramatic than errors in a filter setting.

AudioPhysx can be installed either as a finished, compatible Fab code plugin or from a complete source distribution. This guide describes both approaches, but the current documentation package does not contain or redistribute the paid plugin source. In particular, a ZIP containing only Source/ is not by itself a distributable Unreal plugin: the descriptor and any required build configuration still need to be present.

If you have the Fab package, follow the supported Unreal/Fab installation flow for a verified engine version. Open your project, go to Edit → Plugins and confirm that AudioPhysx is enabled. Restart the Editor when prompted. The exact Launcher/Fab steps should be checked with the final released package, as the commercial installation has not been independently tested during this documentation task.

If you have the source distribution, close Unreal Editor and disable Live Coding. Place the complete plugin directory—including AudioPhysx.uplugin and the Source folder—under YourProject/Plugins/AudioPhysx/. Regenerate project files if necessary, compile the Editor target with the appropriate toolchain, and reopen the project. Do not mix old and new implementations of a node: duplicate registration functions and stale generated headers can cause misleading linker or startup errors.

Check the result in a MetaSound Source. Create a stereo MetaSound Source and search for AP: Random Wave Player or AudioPhysx in the node palette. Confirm the Wave Player has Out Left and Out Right pins, and confirm that AP: Stereo to Mono is available in QoL. This is a useful sanity check that the current stereo build, rather than an older mono DLL, has loaded.

If the plugin appears in the Plugins window but nodes are unavailable, inspect the Editor startup log and the first meaningful build or MetaSound registration message. A successful checkbox state does not prove the module has loaded its native nodes correctly. If you need to clear old build outputs, close the Editor before removing generated Binaries and Intermediate for a clean source rebuild.

A major part of this update changes audio pins from mono to stereo. Back up existing MetaSound assets before refreshing or replacing their AudioPhysx nodes. When you first open an older asset, check every input and output connection rather than assuming Unreal automatically transforms a single mono connection into two independent stereo connections.

New graphs are simplest to author as stereo from the beginning. For world emitters that should remain mono, connect the player or final DSP stage to AP: Stereo to Mono immediately before the Source's mono output. Test the finished graph in the Editor, then in a packaged Development build before relying on it in shipping content.

This example builds an action sound with three stages: a short click, a mechanical movement and a final latch. You will trigger the entire action once, and the Sequence Wave Player will start each recording after the preceding one finishes. The goal is to understand the difference between event wiring, stereo audio wiring and completion without involving any world-based acoustic calculations.

Create a stereo MetaSound Source and import three Wave Assets that you can distinguish easily. They may be mono or stereo recordings, but the AudioPhysx player will expose two channel outputs in the graph. Add AP: Sequence Wave Player from AudioPhysx → Playback and expand the Wave slots to three entries. Put the recordings into those slots in the desired order. The timing comes from the duration of each recording, not from a separate list of manually typed delays.

Connect the Source's On Play trigger to the player's Play input. Connect the player's Out Left to the stereo Source Left output and Out Right to the Source Right output. With Loop Sequence disabled, you can connect the player's On Finished to the MetaSound Source completion trigger when this player is the last audible stage. If you later add Early Reflections or Acoustic Paths, completion should instead account for the tail generated by the downstream processor.

Press Preview. The result should sound like one structured action: click, movement, latch. Now swap the middle recording for a much longer file. The last stage should happen later automatically because the player waits for playback completion. This is why a sequence node can be more robust than scheduling every stage with a hard-coded number of milliseconds.

Try turning on Loop Sequence. The complete three-part action should repeat rather than ending after its final clip. Turn looping off again and press Stop while the middle recording is audible. The stop request cancels the sequence; it is not the same thing as completing the sequence naturally, so do not assume it will issue On Finished.

When you want the three stages to remain in order but use different recordings on each play, move to Random Sequence Wave Player. When the stages should overlap instead of waiting for completion, try Layered Wave Player. Both now output stereo, so the channel-wiring pattern stays familiar.

If you are building a sound that should be precisely located at a point in 3D space, the stereo routing guide explains when to keep both channels and when to convert the final result to mono before spatialization.

l: Stereo routing and deliberate mono conversion
p: AudioPhysx's current design is stereo throughout audio-bearing playback and processing, with a dedicated node for conversion to mono. This is useful because it avoids discarding information before the sound designer has decided whether that information matters. It is not a statement that stereo is always acoustically preferable for every source in a 3D game.

Most Wave Players expose Out Left and Out Right. Acoustic processors commonly expect In Left and In Right and expose Out Left and Out Right again. Their delay and filter histories are separate, so a stereo recording can travel through the chain without being summed into mono at the first stage. The world controls—distance, obstruction, material or speed—are often shared across both channels because they describe one source-to-listener relationship.

A basic full-stereo path might begin with AP: Random Wave Player, continue through AP: Material Transmission, and then feed a stereo MetaSound Source. Connect the player's Left output to the processor's Left input and Right to Right. The processor's Left and Right outputs then connect to the corresponding Source channels. If you accidentally connect the same channel to both inputs, you may hear duplicated mono rather than the original stereo recording.

This also means you can combine source design and processing more freely. A Layered Wave Player can mix a stereo mechanical texture with other recordings; Early Reflections can preserve independent channel history; Dynamic Propagation can delay each stereo channel without first summing them. The effects still have limits and shared physical controls, but stereo content is no longer discarded merely because the plugin's internal renderer has a mono output.

l: When mono is still the better result
p: A small object making a footstep, a gun muzzle report or a collision at a known world position often behaves conceptually as a point source. Unreal's spatializer may be better suited to positioning one mono signal in 3D than a wide stereo recording whose left/right cues were captured or designed for a different listening position. The correct choice depends on the type of sound, the project's spatialization settings and the listening test.

To downmix, place AP: Stereo to Mono after the last stereo processor. Connect Out Left to In Left and Out Right to In Right; then feed its Out Mono into a mono MetaSound output. The node uses a simple sample-by-sample average:

This keeps dual-mono content at the same level rather than summing it 6 dB hotter. It cannot preserve the original stereo field, and opposite-polarity material may cancel during the fold-down. Always audition an important effect in mono before shipping it—especially if you have layered stereo bass or strongly phase-shifted recordings.

If your MetaSound was authored with an older AudioPhysx version, back it up before opening it in the stereo build. Verify the installed module is actually the stereo version, inspect saved node pins, reconnect Left and Right audio paths, and change the MetaSound Source output format only when the finished sound design needs it. Mono-only graphs can use the converter rather than forcing the entire pipeline back to mono.

Do not treat trigger and Float nodes as part of this migration. AP: Doppler Ratio, AP: Float Smoother, AP: Trigger Probability, AP: Trigger Cooldown and AP: Distance Switch do not render audio samples, so their existing event/number pin contracts remain appropriate. AP: Stereo to Mono is the deliberate mono-output exception. Recompile the graph and check real stereo separation using a test recording with noticeably different Left and Right content.
Read the Stereo to Mono node reference for the exact pin names and limitations.

A MetaSound graph contains different kinds of wires because it describes both events and continuous sound. Play, Stop, Reset and On Finished are triggers that represent moments. Out Left, Out Right, In Left and In Right carry the audio sample buffers. A Float such as Distance (cm) or Impact Strength describes a changing control value but does not itself produce sound.

Confusing these responsibilities is a common reason for nodes that appear to work individually but produce silence inside a larger graph. For example, a Wave Player can receive Play and load a valid sample without any audible result if its audio outputs are not connected to the Source. Conversely, an acoustic processor can have both audio channels connected but remain in the wrong state if the required material, route or obstruction input never updates.

l: Stopping and finishing are different events
p: A sound may finish naturally after rendering its final sample, or it may be explicitly cancelled by gameplay. Many AudioPhysx players reserve On Finished for natural completion. For that reason, pressing Stop should not be assumed to fire the same trigger as the end of the recording. Stop Firing on Start Loop End has another meaning: it requests the release phase and allows the ending to play.

Downstream processors introduce another consideration. A Wave Player may finish its original recording while Acoustic Paths is still delivering delayed samples or Early Reflections still has audible taps. In such a graph, the processor's Source Finished input can receive the player's completion signal, and the processor's own On Finished can indicate when the extended audible tail is complete. Ending the MetaSound Source too early cuts off that processing.

When routing the current stereo nodes, move each channel through the intended Left and Right path. The two channels carry separate audio buffer data; duplicating the Left buffer into both inputs is not equivalent to preserving a stereo recording. When you intentionally choose a mono Source, make the fold-down explicit with Stereo to Mono rather than relying on ambiguous routing or connecting a stereo pin into a mono-only input.

Some nodes have expandable pin groups for waves, steps or distance bands. These are part of the authored graph layout. Surface Wave Player can additionally generate pins from project settings. If an interface changes, check the actual pins and connections before saving migrated assets.

Most silent or incorrect AudioPhysx graphs can be diagnosed by working from the simplest part of the chain outward. First make sure a known-good Wave Asset plays through a basic stereo Source with the correct Out Left and Out Right wiring. Only then connect random selection, material routing, time delay or a world acoustic parameter. This separates an asset/import problem from a source-graph problem and from an acoustic-world problem.

When audio is silent, check that the correct start trigger actually reaches the node, that the relevant recording arrays contain playable assets, and that you have connected the outputs to an active MetaSound Source. For players that can reject a request, inspect On Rejected or an index output before assuming Unreal audio itself is failing.

When timing is wrong, distinguish a completion-driven sequence from RPM scheduling. Sequence Wave Player advances only when the current recording finishes. Start Loop End with positive RPM starts middle shots by a fixed interval and needs Stop Firing to enter the release phase. An extra Distance Delay or Acoustic Paths stage can delay the audible output even after the original playback has begun.

When world-driven sound is wrong, print the source-listener distance, physical material, obstruction result or selected acoustic route. Check units carefully: centimetres, metres and metres per second are used for different controls. A perfectly functioning filter cannot make an incorrect material path or invalid world trace meaningful.

Before shipping, test the exact plugin package in a clean project and compare Editor preview with packaged Development and Shipping audio. Include stereo and mono recordings, empty arrays, rapid retriggering and more than one simultaneously active sound. A clean Editor build is important, but it does not prove all runtime platform behaviour.

The current native source contains 24 nodes. They are divided by the job they perform rather than the feature that first inspired them: ten Wave Players for selecting recordings and scheduling playback, five acoustic processors for changing the character of audio, four propagation-related tools (one of which emits only a control value), and five QoL utilities including the new stereo-to-mono converter.

Understanding the difference between these groups is important. A playback node needs an event and usually some Wave Assets. A DSP processor needs an existing audio stream and physical or authored parameters. A control utility may have no audio pins at all because it decides which event passes or what number to use elsewhere. The pages are written to make those responsibilities clear before listing pin names.

l: Navigate by what you are building
How to read the reference pages
p: Each node begins with a practical explanation of the problem it solves. You will then find a more detailed discussion of what the node does to the sound or to the event flow, a real game-audio example, setup guidance and the risks worth testing. The complete pin descriptions are still present in an expandable Exact input and output pins section. They are extracted from the current C++ declarations, so you do not have to trust an older screenshot for the correct pin names.

The stereo convention is consistent across the audio processors: the input is typically In Left and In Right, and the output is Out Left and Out Right. Wave Players generally supply Out Left and Out Right. Control-only nodes are not artificially given audio channels. AP: Stereo to Mono deliberately outputs Out Mono because that is the point of the converter. If you are migrating an older MetaSound, see stereo routing and migration before saving the revised graph.

l: Playback: what should play, and when?
p: A convincing sound library needs more than a folder of recordings. It needs a clear decision about when an event begins, whether recordings overlap, how a variation is chosen, and when the audible result should actually end. AudioPhysx provides several players because these are genuinely different problems: an explosion can use a single variation, a machine may have a fixed mechanical sequence, and an automatic rifle needs a repeatable event cadence independent of individual recording duration.

For one-shot variation, start with Random Wave Player. It can choose a take whenever the game sends an event and allow limited overlap. If repeated events reveal the same recordings too often, Shuffle-Bag Wave Player adds selection history. Both produce stereo audio but do not decide the gameplay timing of the input trigger.

For structured actions, use Sequence Wave Player when every stage should play one specific recording, or Random Sequence Wave Player when each stage can select one of several variations. These wait for the current recording to finish. Layered Wave Player instead combines several recordings at once, with optional per-layer delays, gain and pitch. That difference between sequential and simultaneous audio is fundamental to how the sound will feel.

For held or context-dependent actions, Start Loop End Player manages an introduction, repeated middle and released ending. It now supports RPM-timed overlapping middle shots. Distance Wave Player chooses a recorded perspective using distance. PhysMat Wave Player and Surface Wave Player choose content from material identity, while Flyby Wave Player plays near-miss whizzes and optional cracks using data supplied by the flyby subsystem.

All ten Wave Players now expose Out Left and Out Right. That is a capability, not an instruction to make every source a wide stereo emitter. A localized footstep or weapon report may be better downmixed before 3D positioning, whereas a designed ambience or layered interface effect might benefit from keeping stereo intact. The stereo routing guide covers both cases.
Explore the individual Playback references

l: Acoustics: why does a place change the sound?
p: A recording played through a loudspeaker should not sound identical in every physical situation. It may be blocked by a door, travel around an opening, lose high-frequency detail when the source faces away, or produce an initial set of room reflections. AudioPhysx separates these phenomena into focused processing nodes so you can build only the behaviour needed by a particular sound.

Material Transmission uses an externally supplied obstruction state and material losses to colour a sound through a barrier. Acoustic Paths takes a world-selected route and applies its delay plus low/mid/high frequency losses. The two nodes can sound similar in some situations, but one is an authored material-filter approach and the other is a route-driven processor. Applying both at full strength without a reason can make a source much darker than intended.

Early Reflections is meant to suggest the first short returns from nearby surfaces. It is not the same as pathing through a doorway and is not a complete acoustic room solve. Source Directivity changes the signal with the listener-relative angle, allowing a front-facing emitter to sound more present than when heard from behind. Impact Dynamics shapes transients according to an externally supplied impact strength; it is a DSP stage, not a collision detector.

Every one of these processors now accepts Left and Right audio inputs and emits Left and Right audio outputs. The world/material controls remain shared where that makes physical sense, while channel-specific filter or delay history is kept separate. That lets an effect treat stereo content without reducing it prematurely to one channel. If you later want a mono positional emitter, convert at the end of the relevant chain.

The realism comes from the input data as much as the signal processing. Before adjusting the filter or reflection wetness, verify that the game is sending the correct obstruction, angle, material or impact strength. Blueprint acoustic integration describes where these values come from.

l: Propagation: when sound takes time to reach us
p: Propagation concerns how a sound changes while travelling from its source to the listener. In the real world, an explosion heard at a great distance arrives after its flash, and a moving source can exhibit Doppler shift. In a game, these effects must be balanced against latency, memory and the fact that the level geometry and player motion may update suddenly rather than continuously.

Distance Delay captures a travel-time delay based on distance and sound speed. It works well for discrete events whose distance can be latched. Dynamic Propagation changes the delay continuously for a moving source and includes smoothing and jump handling to keep the audible result controlled. Both are stereo DSP nodes and maintain separate channel delay histories.

Doppler Ratio computes a pitch multiplier from relative radial motion. It does not output audio—there is no reason to manufacture left and right audio channels for a single numeric ratio. Use it when another playback stage needs a pitch control, and avoid applying it again to a sound whose Dynamic Propagation has already introduced Doppler-like movement.

Atmosphere Absorption adjusts high-frequency content according to travelled distance and environmental conditions. It is separate from a wall-transmission filter and separate from ordinary source volume attenuation. In some projects Unreal's own air absorption may already be active, so compare the complete chain before using both systems together.

These are physically motivated approximations, not guaranteed measurements of the acoustic field in your level. A reliable design uses the right units and limits processing to what the listener can actually perceive. The individual references discuss centimetres, metres per second and buffer capacities in detail.

Not everything in AudioPhysx needs to process audio samples. Many MetaSounds become difficult to maintain because the same housekeeping logic is rebuilt repeatedly: a trigger should only pass every few hundred milliseconds, an occasional detail should only fire sometimes, or a filter parameter should move smoothly instead of jumping between values. The QoL nodes solve those narrow problems and can be connected to any suitable playback or processing chain.

Trigger Cooldown limits how often an event can pass. Trigger Probability accepts some events at a specified chance. Float Smoother conditions a block-rate numeric value using rise and fall response. Distance Switch routes a trigger into the appropriate distance band instead of embedding several nested branch nodes in every MetaSound. All four are intentionally control-only; they do not need stereo outputs.

The new Stereo to Mono is the exception. It accepts In Left and In Right and emits Out Mono using a conservative average. This is useful because the other AudioPhysx audio nodes are stereo by default. If the end of a graph needs a mono audio buffer, you can explicitly place the converter there rather than giving up stereo content in the first Wave Player.

A good QoL graph should remain easy to read. For example, a gameplay event might pass through a short cooldown and then a probability gate before triggering an optional mechanical rattle. Each control has one job. Overusing them can conceal a gameplay bug just as easily as it can clean up an audio graph, so test the underlying events before adding complicated gating logic.

AudioPhysx separates gameplay-side world queries from audio rendering. One consequence is that some MetaSound inputs are fed by named parameters or registered interfaces rather than being authored independently in each graph. These names and data types are contracts. They should not be approximated by creating visually similar inputs with arbitrary spelling.

The current source includes a selected-route Float Array named AP.AcousticRoute.Selected. It is intended for the Acoustic Paths processor, and the values must follow the same order as the source-side contract:

The world path solver decides whether direct or around-obstacle sound should be selected; the MetaSound processor applies the corresponding delay and three-band loss. Keeping the route together in one array reduces the possibility that the delay comes from a different query update than the spectral losses. The convenience does make the ordering more important, so verify the exact array before trying to correct an unexpected filter result.

Other AudioPhysx systems expose atmosphere, transmission, impact and propagation values through their current interfaces. Where an installed build supplies those interfaces, use the actual registered names and types. Do not construct an independent parameter solely from an old screenshot if the current interface has changed. MetaSound asset interface migrations and configurable surface-route changes can affect how saved graphs reconnect.

The flyby subsystem has a separate set of five named Float inputs beginning with AP.Flyby.. Those are documented on the Flyby Blueprint page. All such interfaces carry control values or triggers: they do not change the fact that the audio processors themselves now carry stereo Left and Right buffers.

c: [delay ms, low loss dB, mid loss dB, high loss dB]

p: MetaSound processes audio and audio-rate events, but it does not automatically know where a projectile travelled, what wall is between a source and listener, or which Physical Material was returned by a collision query. AudioPhysx uses Blueprint-accessible helpers, world subsystems and Actor components to provide that information without moving world-geometry work onto the audio rendering thread.

The recommended process is to verify the game data before processing the sound. If an acoustic filter seems wrong, print the obstruction flag or selected path. If a material player chooses the fallback recordings, print the material identifier from the hit result. If a flyby never plays, first check whether the path passed within the audible radius. This separates gameplay setup problems from decoding and DSP issues.

The stereo conversion does not require a new Blueprint API: these helpers still supply sound assets and control data, while the internal MetaSound graph now connects Left and Right audio buffers. Refer to stereo routing when authoring the Source itself.

l: Projectile flybys from a path segment
p: A useful projectile near-miss sound should represent a projectile that actually passed near the listener, not every time any weapon fired. AudioPhysx's flyby helper accepts the start and end of a projectile path segment, its speed, and an audible radius. It can calculate the point of closest approach and an approximate arrival time. The audio renderer then uses that result to play a whizz and, where appropriate, a shock-like crack.

The public Blueprint API exposes AP: Calculate Flyby, which returns an FAPFlybyResult with values such as bAudible, bShockWave, ClosestPoint, DistanceMeters, SpeedMetersPerSecond, Intensity and ArrivalSeconds. This is valuable for debugging because it lets you inspect the geometry and acoustic decision without immediately scheduling audio. AP: Play Projectile Flyby combines the calculation with world-level scheduling; a true return means the request was accepted for scheduling, not that the listener has already heard the resulting sound.

Create a stereo MetaSound Source and add AP: Flyby Wave Player. Supply one or more Whizz Waves and optionally Crack Waves. Connect Out Left and Out Right to the Source's corresponding stereo outputs. Expose the following Float inputs with precisely these names, as used by the current flyby world subsystem:
AP.Flyby.DistanceM → Distance (m)
AP.Flyby.SpeedMps → Speed (m/s)
AP.Flyby.Intensity → Intensity
AP.Flyby.SpeedOfSoundMps → Speed of Sound (m/s)
AP.Flyby.Shock → Shock

These are parameter-name contracts, not arbitrary labels. A name that looks nearly identical but differs in punctuation or capitalization should not be assumed to update the intended MetaSound input. The subsystem sets these controls before starting the sound.

For a hitscan weapon, use the muzzle or trace start as PathStart, and the hit location or maximum trace end as PathEnd. Pass the final MetaSound Source as FlybyMetaSound. Provide projectile speed in metres per second and the audible radius in metres. A newly submitted hitscan event normally has a path age of zero.

For moving projectiles, provide successive path segments from the projectile's actual movement. ProjectileInstance should represent one distinct projectile, not the weapon that fires many rounds, because the world subsystem may use it to suppress duplicate near misses. PathAgeSeconds describes when the submitted segment occurred relative to the query; incorrect values may change the apparent arrival timing.

Start with an obviously close path and print the calculation result. Next submit a path outside the audible radius, then compare slower and faster projectiles. Only after the geometry makes sense should you tune the recordings and their stereo output. A close flyby may still be appropriate as a mono spatialized source in some projects; Stereo to Mono provides that option downstream.

The current acoustic model is deliberately approximate: it assumes simplified path and speed behaviour rather than a full shock-front or trajectory simulation. Measure the finished result by listening in your own game and check for duplicates, unrealistic near-miss thresholds and excessively loud cracks.

l: Querying sound routes through the level
p: A line from source to listener may be clear, obstructed by a wall or partly bypassed through an opening. AudioPhysx provides a game-thread acoustic path solver to estimate how these possibilities affect the sound. The result is deliberately separate from the MetaSound render thread: scene traces and geometry queries belong with the game world, while stereo DSP nodes process the returned control values.

The Blueprint library exposes AP: Query Acoustic Path, taking a world context, source location, listener location and optional source actor. Its result describes obstruction state, surface type, barrier count, acoustic-material use and measured thickness, plus direct-path delay and low/mid/high losses. It can additionally describe an around-obstacle candidate, including a possible emitter position and its estimated delay and frequency losses.

A particularly important distinction is bAroundPathValid versus bAroundPathSelected. Valid means the solver found a candidate. Selected means it considers that candidate preferable according to the available losses and configuration. The corresponding Acoustic Paths MetaSound node renders one selected route rather than automatically duplicating the signal into direct and around channels.

For testing, build a small scene with a sound source, listener and a single blocking surface. Query with a clear path first, then move the listener behind the barrier. Print the obstruction flag, barrier count, direct delay and band losses. Once those results are understandable, add an opening or Acoustic Portal and inspect whether a valid and selected alternate route appears. These experiments reveal much more than immediately trying to tune filter parameters by ear.

The selected route contract passed to the audio processor is a compact four-value Float Array: delay milliseconds, low loss dB, mid loss dB, high loss dB. The order is part of the interface. Connect the stereo source signal to Acoustic Paths, feed the selected array, and route completion through the processor when it still has delayed audio to release. When hearing something odd, first confirm the exact four values printed from the world-side calculation.

Because world queries cost CPU time, AudioPhysx has per-tick scheduling and ray budgets. Querying every emitter every rendered sample would be inappropriate. Use managed update intervals and realistic emitter counts, profile packaged-game performance, and avoid assigning the highest query detail to effects whose difference cannot be heard in the final mix.

Many AudioPhysx sounds begin in ordinary gameplay code. A character performs an interaction, a projectile hits a surface, or a persistent emitter needs to follow an Actor. The Blueprint playback library provides convenience operations to connect those events to audio while allowing optional acoustic management when the project needs it.

AP: Play Physical Sound accepts a sound asset and world location, with a source rotation, volume and relevant optional acoustic settings supplied through its function signature. It is useful when the event has a known position and you do not want to create a dedicated audio Actor for every occurrence. AP: Play Physical Impact is related, but takes an FHitResult so the event can use hit-location information already produced by gameplay.

These functions do not generate recordings or automatically configure a MetaSound graph. Supply a valid USoundBase asset with the desired Wave Players and processing. After the stereo upgrade, the inside of that MetaSound may be stereo or deliberately folded down to mono; the Blueprint call still works with the sound asset rather than its individual audio pins.

For sounds that continue playing as the world changes, AP: Register Audio Component can associate an existing UAudioComponent with managed AudioPhysx parameter updates, optionally enabling obstruction tracing. When the source is no longer relevant, AP: Unregister Audio Component removes that registration. Use component lifetime deliberately rather than leaving an unlimited number of emitters active in an otherwise quiet scene.

The separate AP: Set World Environment operation supplies temperature, humidity and pressure to the AudioPhysx world environment. These values can influence appropriate acoustic calculations, but setting them does not automatically make every sound in the project change. Only nodes and registered systems that use those parameters can render a corresponding audible difference.

A useful first test is to create a known-good stereo MetaSound with one Random Wave Player, call Play Physical Sound at a visible world location, and confirm that you hear it as expected. Test that baseline before turning on any obstruction or propagation processing. If the sound fails only after adding acoustic queries, you have narrowed the problem to the additional data rather than decoding, module loading or the basic sound asset.

AudioPhysx includes optional components that associate sounds, physical obstacles and openings with real level objects. They are designed to let a managed acoustic system reason about where a sound begins and what it passes through. You do not need to attach all these components to use Random Wave Player or other ordinary playback nodes.

UAPSpatialAudioEmitterComponent represents a managed source with a sound asset, optional attenuation asset and obstruction-trace behaviour. It is a practical starting point for a sound that stays in the world while the listener or emitter moves. UAPAcousticBarrierComponent associates an acoustic material, a target primitive and optional thickness override with level geometry. The geometry and collision still have to be configured correctly, because the component cannot measure useful thickness from an object that the relevant trace never intersects.

UAPAcousticPortalComponent represents a possible passage with extra low, mid and high frequency losses, which the around-path system can consider when enabled and available. It should not be mistaken for a full portal-based reverb engine. UAPPhysicsBridgeComponent provides another link between game-side state and audio parameters for supported physics/environment workflows; it is not required for a simple standalone Wave Player.

Create two simple spaces connected by a doorway, place one looping source in the first room, and put the listener in the second. Begin with no obstruction, then add a wall primitive with a valid Acoustic Barrier component and suitable collision. Use the Blueprint path query to inspect whether the wall is recognized. Only after the direct path works should you add the Portal near the opening and look for around-path candidates.

The test should be as controlled as possible. Do not begin with a complex production level containing hundreds of intersecting meshes and several overlapping emitters. A small map makes it clear whether a change in sound comes from barrier properties, path selection, a manually authored filter or Unreal's normal attenuation.

Since the world system operates on scheduled updates and query budgets, you should also profile a realistic count of active sources. A feature can sound convincing in a room with one emitter and still require careful update limits to perform acceptably in a dense game environment.

l: Acoustic materials, thickness and performance settings
p: An Acoustic Physical Material describes the model you want AudioPhysx to use for a surface's sound-transmission behaviour. The current UAPAcousticPhysicalMaterial derives from Unreal's Physical Material and adds acoustic parameters such as density, longitudinal sound speed, internal damping, transmission loss, reference thickness, absorption and scattering. It is an authorable model, not a laboratory measurement automatically extracted from your mesh.

When enabled, the material can use an authored low/mid/high transmission-loss description or an approximate mass-law approach. Authored losses are useful when a sound designer knows the listening result they want and wants reproducible control. The alternative model uses material-related values to derive an estimate. Either approach must be judged by what the gameplay geometry and audio routing actually supply; a heavy-looking object with the wrong collision or missing material assignment may contribute no meaningful acoustic data.

l: Set up the model in stages
p: First make sure a trace identifies the intended primitive or Physical Material. Then assign an Acoustic Barrier component or supported acoustic material configuration. Start with an easily heard contrast between a clear and blocked source, using reasonable thickness and a clear three-band loss difference. Once the result works, refine density, damping, reference thickness and any optional scattering or absorption data that the chosen processing path actually uses.

UAPAudioSettings contains environment values, surface routes and performance limits. The current source exposes emitter updates per tick, obstruction traces per tick, scheduled acoustic-ray budgets, query refresh intervals, maximum barrier layers, thickness measurement controls and optional around-obstacle paths. These settings exist because acoustic world queries must remain predictable as the number of active emitters increases.

A final important setting concerns Surface Audio routes. AP: Surface Wave Player can generate input pins from the configured enabled surfaces. Changes to that list can affect existing graph interfaces, so back up and review affected MetaSound assets before assuming a new surface configuration will be harmless. The stereo upgrade is another independent interface change: reconnect both channel outputs in migrated graphs, and verify saved graphs before publishing the plugin to customers.

Node reference pages explain individual tools; the examples show how several parts fit together in an actual listening task. They deliberately begin with ordinary Wave Assets and small MetaSound graphs rather than a large demonstration project that needs dozens of dependencies. Once you understand the basic routing, you can replace the test sounds with your game's own authored content.

For playback, try randomized one-shots or an automatic weapon with RPM. These show the distinction between selecting a recording and scheduling it in time. A random multi-stage action demonstrates how each stage can vary while retaining the order of the action. The material footstep recipe connects gameplay surface data to sound selection.

For world-reactive audio, the flyby exercise separates projectile geometry from audio playback, while the acoustic obstruction example compares a simple authored barrier filter with a selected world route. Both are designed to be understood by printing the gameplay result before adjusting the sound.

These recipes use the new stereo conventions. Unless a specific example intentionally downmixes, audio-bearing connections should run Left to Left and Right to Right. If you are building a precisely localized point emitter, the stereo routing guide explains when and how to introduce Stereo to Mono at the end of the chain.

Use your own or appropriately licensed recordings for these exercises. A test that sounds poor because the assets contain leading silence, mismatched loudness or phase problems is not a reliable evaluation of the node's actual timing and processing behaviour.
Primary AudioPhysx tools: AP: Random Wave Player

A good example is a listening experiment, not just a screenshot of connected pins. This exercise explains what content to prepare, which signals the graph needs, and what result you should listen for before increasing complexity.

Use several recordings of one physical event, such as a handful of metal objects being moved or several punches on the same surface. Import the files as Wave Assets and trim them so their transients begin consistently. Aim for roughly similar perceived level; the player can choose a recording but cannot magically make radically different source edits sound like one cohesive event.

l: Assemble the MetaSound and test it
p: Add a Random Wave Player to a stereo Source and connect the recording array to Waves. Connect the event trigger to Play, then route Out Left and Out Right to the stereo output. Enable No Immediate Repeat when you have multiple valid takes and want to reduce consecutive identical choices. Choose a Max Voices setting appropriate to the likely overlap and listen to a rapid burst of triggers, not just one click.

l: Judge the result in a game
p: You should hear the same kind of event with subtle natural differences. If one take leaps out of the mix or contains a long tail that conflicts with the next event, correct the source asset or reduce overlap deliberately. For a strictly positioned sound, try converting the completed stereo result to mono before spatialization and compare the two presentations.

A repeatable test in a small scene is more valuable than adding several processors at once. Check the Source's channel layout and all completion events before moving the same graph into a large level. If the audio will ultimately be positioned as a mono point source, audition the Stereo to Mono version as well as the full stereo path.
Browse the full node reference for exact control types and limitations.
Primary AudioPhysx tools: AP: Start Loop End Player

A good example is a listening experiment, not just a screenshot of connected pins. This exercise explains what content to prepare, which signals the graph needs, and what result you should listen for before increasing complexity.

Collect a short introductory attack or weapon mechanism, several main gunshot variations and one or more release/tail recordings. Keep the main recordings in a consistent tonal family. A gunshot that rings for 250 ms does not need to be cut to 100 ms just because the weapon fires at 600 rounds per minute; the scheduler is designed to let the recordings overlap.

l: Assemble the MetaSound and test it
p: Create a stereo Source and add Start Loop End Player. Fill Start Waves, Loop Waves and End Waves. Route gameplay press to Start Firing and release to Stop Firing, then connect Left/Right audio and final completion. Set RPM to 600 and audition a sustained hold: once the introductory recording finishes, middle shots should be scheduled roughly every 100 ms. Test Immediate Release both on and off to hear whether active shots fade quickly or finish before the ending begins.

l: Judge the result in a game
p: A convincing automatic weapon should communicate a stable firing rhythm while allowing individual shot bodies and tails to overlap. The source has a bounded twelve-voice middle pool, so extremely high RPM plus long clips can saturate it and cause new scheduled shots to be skipped. If the event never finishes, check that Stop Firing actually arrives; a missing release event is not an audio-decoder problem.

A repeatable test in a small scene is more valuable than adding several processors at once. Check the Source's channel layout and all completion events before moving the same graph into a large level. If the audio will ultimately be positioned as a mono point source, audition the Stereo to Mono version as well as the full stereo path.

Primary AudioPhysx tools: AP: Random Sequence Wave Player

A good example is a listening experiment, not just a screenshot of connected pins. This exercise explains what content to prepare, which signals the graph needs, and what result you should listen for before increasing complexity.

Imagine a powered door that makes three recognizably ordered sounds: a button or access click, the motor moving, and a final latch. Record several alternatives for each distinct phase. Store all opening clicks in one array, all motor variations in a second, and all closing clunks in a third. Keeping the arrays semantically separate is more important than their exact size.

l: Assemble the MetaSound and test it
p: Create a stereo Source with Random Sequence Wave Player and expand it to three array steps. Connect the arrays in the desired order, route Play from one interaction trigger, then connect both stereo audio outputs. With Loop Sequence disabled, On Finished can end the Source after the last phase. Trigger the action repeatedly and listen to how the selected recordings change without changing the overall structure.

l: Judge the result in a game
p: The player waits for the chosen recording in one phase to finish before beginning the next. That makes this much easier to maintain than a chain of hard-coded delays when you replace assets later. If you actually need multiple stages to sound at once, use Layered Wave Player instead; that is a mixing problem, not a sequencing problem.

Primary AudioPhysx tools: AP: Surface or PhysMat Wave Player

A good example is a listening experiment, not just a screenshot of connected pins. This exercise explains what content to prepare, which signals the graph needs, and what result you should listen for before increasing complexity.

Start with two clearly different ground types, such as stone and grass, and prepare several footstep recordings for each. The character's animation or gameplay system supplies the foot-contact timing; AudioPhysx is responsible for choosing an appropriate recording after the ground has been identified. Do not debug the Wave Player before verifying that your trace returns the expected surface identifier.

l: Assemble the MetaSound and test it
p: For broad categories, configure Surface Audio routes and use Surface Wave Player with the Hit Surface Type integer. For specific Physical Material assets, use PhysMat Wave Player with the exact Hit PhysMat Path. In either case, assign a default recording pool for unmatched material information, then connect Play, Out Left and Out Right. Walk over both known materials and an intentionally unmapped surface while printing the gameplay result.

l: Judge the result in a game
p: Surface type and Physical Material path represent different levels of detail; pick the one your game actually uses. A stereo recording may be suitable as part of a designed close-up effect, but a character's footstep as a small point source is also a good candidate for a final Stereo to Mono downmix. Listen in the game's actual spatialization environment rather than assuming one format will always be better.

Primary AudioPhysx tools: AP: Flyby Wave Player + Blueprint helper

A good example is a listening experiment, not just a screenshot of connected pins. This exercise explains what content to prepare, which signals the graph needs, and what result you should listen for before increasing complexity.

A near miss should be driven by a projectile path rather than by the fact that a gun was fired. Start with a straight hitscan segment that passes deliberately beside the listener and a second segment that clearly misses the audible radius. Choose a couple of whizz recordings and optionally separate crack recordings. Their editing and apparent source distance will strongly influence the perceived quality of the result.

l: Assemble the MetaSound and test it
p: Set up a stereo Source with Flyby Wave Player and the five exact AP.Flyby.* Float inputs described in the Blueprint flyby guide. Call AP: Calculate Flyby first and print bAudible, closest distance and shock state. When those values match the geometry, use AP: Play Projectile Flyby to schedule the Source for an accepted path. Feed the actual shot start, end and metres-per-second speed to the helper.

l: Judge the result in a game
p: Compare close, distant, slower and faster passes. The crack layer should follow the computed shock request rather than playing on every whizz. If a moving projectile produces duplicate flybys, review the ProjectileInstance you supply for duplicate suppression. Remember that the helper uses a simplified constant-speed acoustic model, not an exact physical shock-front simulation.

Primary AudioPhysx tools: AP: Material Transmission or Acoustic Paths

A good example is a listening experiment, not just a screenshot of connected pins. This exercise explains what content to prepare, which signals the graph needs, and what result you should listen for before increasing complexity.

Use a short, bright source such as speech, a hand clap or a mechanical impact. A strong high-frequency component makes it easier to hear what the obstruction processor changes. Put the source behind a simple wall and establish a clear listening reference before adding effects. When the recording is already very dull, it may be difficult to hear the difference between correct transmission and an ineffective setup.

l: Assemble the MetaSound and test it
p: For the simplest comparison, use Material Transmission with a controlled Obstructed Boolean and set the high-band loss larger than the low-band loss. Connect In Left and In Right, then the processed stereo outputs. For world-selected path processing, first print the route from the acoustic Blueprint query and feed its four-value Float Array into Acoustic Paths. Pass the upstream completion trigger into Source Finished so delayed audio is not cut off.

l: Judge the result in a game
p: The blocked version should generally become quieter and less bright while still sounding like the same source. If it is overly muffled, check whether Unreal's native occlusion is also active. If the effect appears too late, check the path delay and the amount of delay buffering reserved by the node. A world-derived path model is only as reliable as its collision data and query settings.

AudioPhysx adds native audio players, world-query integrations and DSP nodes to Unreal Engine, so troubleshooting is easiest when you separate build and registration, event and asset playback, and world-derived control data. An Editor plugin that is enabled but has missing nodes suggests a different problem from a Wave Player that starts but is not routed to any Source output.

The troubleshooting guide starts from those distinctions. The FAQ explains why audio nodes are now stereo, how to choose mono spatialization, how physics-related helpers use gameplay data, and which features are actually included in the current source. The compatibility page deliberately distinguishes an intended engine target from a verified, packaged commercial build. Changelog records this documentation baseline without inventing a Fab release version.

When reporting a problem, include the exact Unreal Engine version, plugin version or source snapshot, the node or Blueprint function involved, and a minimal reproduction. For a build issue, the first meaningful compiler or linker error is normally more useful than the last line of the build log. For a playback issue, a small screenshot showing Play, both audio channels and completion wiring is often more useful than a full screenshot of a huge production graph.

When an effect does not behave as expected, debug from the outside in. First verify Unreal can play the chosen recording. Then verify the MetaSound receives its starting trigger. Next confirm the expected Left and Right audio buffers reach the Source output. Only after this works should you investigate acoustic path data, material configuration, voice limits or the extra DSP stages in the chain. That process may feel slower than changing settings randomly, but it usually identifies the real problem with fewer false fixes.

l: Missing nodes, silence or incorrect audio layout
p: If the AudioPhysx nodes do not appear in the palette, check Edit → Plugins and confirm that the correct native module loaded. After replacing source files, close Unreal Editor, disable Live Coding and rebuild for the intended engine version. A duplicate .cpp file or a stale binary from an older plugin version can make registration confusing even if the project appears to launch normally.

If a node is present but silent, use one known-good Wave Asset and a simple Source. Make sure the requested array actually contains playable recordings, Play reaches the correct input and both Out Left and Out Right are connected as intended. The stereo upgrade may leave older saved graphs with missing or stale mono connections. A Source set to Stereo needs the correct output channel routing; a Source deliberately set to Mono needs an explicit Stereo to Mono path when using AudioPhysx's stereo outputs.

If a player offers On Rejected, observe it while testing. It can distinguish a failed start request from an audible voice that happens to be attenuated or spatialized out of hearing range. Check the Selected Index and active-voice diagnostics where those are provided.

Sequence Wave Player advances after one recording actually finishes. Random Sequence makes a new selection at each stage and follows the same completion-driven timing. Start Loop End is different: its positive RPM setting starts middle shots at scheduled intervals and waits for Stop Firing before entering its ending phase. If you never supply that release event, it is not expected to finish like an ordinary one-shot.

A downstream Acoustic Paths or Early Reflections node may continue to produce audio after the original Wave Player finishes. Pass the player's On Finished to Source Finished on the processor and use the processor's own completion output where appropriate. Otherwise a Source-level completion connection can kill the final delayed samples. Conversely, do not automatically assume explicit Stop emits a natural-completion trigger; the detailed node pages explain cancellation behaviour.

l: Incorrect physics, material or environment behaviour
p: If PhysMat Wave Player always uses the fallback pool, print the exact Physical Material asset path coming from the hit result. If Surface Wave Player selects the wrong pool, check the EPhysicalSurface integer and the configured route list. Changes to surface-specific routes can alter dynamic pins, so back up and inspect affected MetaSound assets after changing those settings.

If flyby playback does not happen, call AP: Calculate Flyby and inspect bAudible, closest distance and shock state before scheduling audio. The path endpoints use Unreal world coordinates, while the audible radius and speed inputs use metres and metres per second. If Acoustic Paths sounds too dark or delayed, inspect the selected four-value route array and make sure its order is delay, low loss, mid loss, high loss. Do not assume a well-functioning filter can correct wrong world data.

l: Editor works but packaged game does not
p: A successful Editor compile or MetaSound preview is not complete runtime verification. Test a clean installation in a new project and package Development and Shipping configurations for each platform you intend to claim. Verify cooked Wave Assets, module loading, engine API compatibility and audio-device behaviour with the exact commercial distribution rather than a development folder that may contain extra files.

When asking for help, share a minimal graph with the relevant pin connections and the first meaningful log error. Keep personal project paths, account details and client or private data out of public issue reports.

Why make all the audio nodes stereo? The previous mono-first design forced information out of a stereo recording before a sound designer had decided whether that information was useful. The updated Wave Players and DSP processors preserve Left and Right channels, making it possible to author wider layered effects and process stereo ambience without an early downmix. This is a signal-path capability, not a requirement that every positional world sound remain stereo. A small point-source effect may still be better downmixed before Unreal spatialization.

Does Stereo to Mono destroy stereo information? Yes, deliberately. It produces one mono signal by averaging the channels, 0.5 × (Left + Right). That avoids the simple level increase from adding two identical channels, but opposite-polarity content may cancel. It also cannot restore any original stereo image after the fold-down. Use it near the end of the graph when that format is appropriate, and listen to the result.

Why do some AudioPhysx nodes still have no Left and Right outputs? Trigger Cooldown, Trigger Probability, Float Smoother, Dynamic Distance Switch and Doppler Ratio are controls or event processors, not audio renderers. A trigger or single pitch ratio does not become a two-channel sound just because a nearby Wave Player is stereo. Their outputs remain correctly typed for the data they represent.

Does AudioPhysx replace MetaSounds or Unreal spatialization? No. It adds focused native tools to the existing Unreal audio pipeline. Source layouts, attenuation, concurrency and spatialization remain important. AudioPhysx helps decide which recording to play, what effect to apply and how game information reaches that processing.

Do the acoustic nodes perform a fully accurate world simulation? No. They combine physically inspired calculations with practical perceptual approximations. For example, Early Reflections creates synthetic taps rather than measuring every real surface, and the flyby solver uses a simplified constant-speed path. Reliable results depend on good recording content, geometry data, material values and informed mixing decisions.

Do I need Chaos? The flyby system can evaluate supplied projectile path segments without building a special Chaos rigid-body simulation. Acoustic queries rely on world geometry and collision information, but they are not themselves a requirement to run Chaos physics for every sound event.

Can AudioPhysx be used with Sound Cues? The native node set inspected for this edition is a MetaSound library, with Blueprint helpers available for sound assets. Dedicated custom Sound Cue QoL nodes are planned but not included in the reviewed source. Unreal's own Sound Cues remain available separately.

Will this automatically work with Unreal Engine 6? No UE6 support is verified or promised. The playback system still uses some Unreal-internal APIs behind a private adapter, and changes in future engine versions may require plugin updates. The compatibility matrix should be updated only after testing the actual submitted package.

These pages are based on the AudioPhysx UE 5.8.4 source package uploaded for this documentation revision. They describe what is present in the code and how it is intended to be used. They do not constitute independent evidence that the plugin compiles, auditions or packages successfully in every target configuration. Before marketing a Fab release, run a clean-project installation and verify the exact shipping archive rather than a development source tree with additional local dependencies.

Source target: Unreal Engine 5.8.4. New audio convention: stereo playback/DSP output, with the explicit Stereo to Mono converter. Pending verification: compilation and audio tests on the exact release archive, clean Blueprint-only project installation, packaged Development and Shipping builds, and any operating system or Unreal Engine version intended to be listed as supported. Not claimed: automatic compatibility with future UE6 releases or untested target platforms.

l: What to test before listing a supported version
p: Create a fresh project with the intended supported engine, install only the plugin files customers will receive and confirm that all native node registrations appear. Test stereo separation using a Wave Asset with different Left and Right content. Test the Stereo to Mono average, including the effect of phase cancellation. Exercise Random Wave Player with overlapping voices, Sequence and Random Sequence with varying recording lengths, and Start Loop End at zero and positive RPM with both release settings.

Then test one representative acoustic processor with a stereo input, a managed acoustic path with an actual barrier and a flyby triggered by a real path segment. Use a Development package to diagnose unexpected behaviour, then verify a Shipping package. Performance should be tested with a realistic count of emitters and voices, not just one preview graph.

The code includes some engine-internal playback dependencies, dynamic configurable pin layouts and simplified acoustic models. A private playback adapter reduces the number of future engine-specific call sites but does not guarantee cross-version compatibility. These are practical engineering boundaries to document, not excuses to claim functionality without listening tests.

For the final commercial documentation, replace this provisional statement with a dated matrix of engine version, operating system, build configuration and verified result. Add only combinations you have actually tested. If a future engine requires source changes, describe the new compatible release instead of implying that a binary built for an older engine must work unchanged.

Stereo documentation revision — 27 November 2026. The site now describes 24 current native MetaSound nodes, including the new AP: Stereo to Mono converter. References use the updated In Left, In Right, Out Left and Out Right audio paths where present. The prose has been rewritten to explain behaviour, game-audio applications and practical limitations in full paragraphs rather than relying on repetitive tables or isolated pin labels. An accompanying visual stylesheet reduces oversized headings and adds restrained AudioPhysx blue/teal accents.

Previous playback development. The plugin source includes a shared Wave Player backend adapter, specialized selection and sequencing players, material-aware playback, projectile flybys and acoustic routing helpers. Start Loop End includes RPM-based scheduling as well as its older completion-based middle mode.

This entry records the source and documentation basis. It is not a claim that a Fab v1.0 package has been submitted, validated for Shipping or released. When a commercial package exists, it should receive an explicit version number, release date, supported-engine matrix and meaningful change notes based on that actual binary/source archive.
